name: Faded Blue
lede: Faded Blue pairs the modifier "faded" with plain blue, naming a washed-out, greyed blue that books tie to monks' habits and to work clothes worn in protest.

sections.title: A modifier on blue, with older echoes
sections.body: Faded Blue pairs "faded" with [[blue]], the xkcd 2010 color-naming survey's term for this washed-out, greyed blue [1]. The exact compound is the survey's; the words themselves are older. Pastoureau writes that Cistercian and Benedictine monks, unable to afford a solid black for their habits, often wore "more or less faded blue" instead [2]. Balfour-Paul notes that faded blue work clothes, most famously blue denim jeans, were later worn deliberately as an anti-establishment statement [3]. Its nearest named look-alikes in our library are [[clear-cadet-blue]], [[dusty-blue]] and [[dusty-blue]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this blue in 0.56 percent of the 23,781 paintings we have, 134 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 86 [5]. That is more common than 57 percent of the named colors in our archive [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent across the 86 paintings where it appears [5]. The earliest match in our archive is dated 1426, nearly six centuries before the name's own earliest record of 2010; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [5].

questions.q: What does Balfour-Paul say faded blue work clothes, like denim jeans, came to represent?
True or false: Pastoureau writes that some monks wore faded blue instead of true black.

openers: Some monks wore faded blue instead of true black, since a solid black dye cost too much.
